nameStory: The Greater White-fronted Goose gets its name from the distinctive white patch of feathers that borders the base of its bill, like a pale forehead marking. The scientific name 'albifrons' literally means 'white forehead' in Latin, from 'albus' (white) and 'frons' (forehead). Many hunters and birders prefer the nickname 'specklebelly' because of the bird's striking salt-and-pepper breast markings that are even more noticeable than the white face patch.
description: The Greater White-fronted Goose is a medium-sized goose that's slightly smaller than a Canada Goose but larger than most ducks. Adults are grayish-brown overall with a distinctive white patch above the bill and bold black barring across the belly that creates a speckled or salt-and-pepper appearance. These Arctic-breeding geese are long-distance migrants that pass through New England during spring and fall, often joining flocks of Canada Geese in fields and wetlands. Their orange legs and bills help distinguish them from other brown geese you might encounter.

idTips.label: White forehead patch
idTips.description: Look for a bright white band of feathers above the orange bill, creating a distinctive 'white forehead' that stands out against the brown head

idTips.label: Speckled belly markings
idTips.description: Adults show bold black bars and spots across the light-colored breast and belly, creating a distinctive salt-and-pepper or speckled appearance that's visible even at a distance

idTips.label: Orange bill and legs
idTips.description: The bill is bright orange-yellow and feels smooth to the touch, while the legs are a similar orange color - much brighter than the duller bills of Canada Geese

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than Canada Geese when seen together, with a shorter neck and rounder head profile

idTips.label: Overall coloration
idTips.description: Grayish-brown body with darker wings and a lighter, buffy-colored breast that shows the black markings well

habitat: In New England, Greater White-fronted Geese are typically found in agricultural fields, flooded meadows, and shallow wetlands during migration periods. They often feed in cornfields, pastures, and grassy areas near water, sometimes mixing with flocks of Canada Geese. Look for them around coastal marshes, farm ponds, and large river valleys where they can find both food and roosting sites.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in March and April when flocks pass through heading to Arctic breeding grounds. Look for them in recently flooded fields and early green pastures where they feed on emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer as they breed far north in the Arctic tundra. Any summer sightings would be unusual stragglers or injured birds.
seasonality.fall: More commonly seen during fall migration from September through November, often in mixed flocks with Canada Geese. They're attracted to harvested corn and grain fields.
seasonality.winter: Uncommon but possible in mild winters, especially along the coast. Most continue south to warmer regions, but a few may linger around open water and available food sources.

funFact: These geese can live over 20 years and return to the exact same Arctic breeding territories each year, with some individuals making round-trip migrations of over 5,000 miles annually - that's like flying from New York to London and back every single year of their lives!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Canada Geese when the white forehead isn't clearly visible, but remember 'speckled belly, orange bill' - Canada Geese have solid dark breasts and black bills. Young birds lack the white forehead patch but still show some belly speckling and orange leg color.
contextualKnowledge: The name can be confusing because there's also a Lesser White-fronted Goose in Europe and Asia, but the 'Greater' refers to size comparison with that species. In North America, when people say 'White-fronted Goose' they almost always mean this Greater species.
compareHints: Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings. They're much smaller than the rare Greylag Goose and lack the pink bill and legs of Pink-footed Geese. The speckled belly pattern is unique among the gray geese and makes identification straightforward once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips.
Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese.
Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill.
Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose.
